headline: DeepSeek Enters Unitree’s Vendor Queue
deck: DeepSeek’s locked Unitree allocation covers 2.31% of the IPO issue and 0.2308% of the enlarged company. The filing creates reciprocal procurement preferences, while the product, pilot and data pipeline remain absent.
body: DeepSeek received 933,399 Unitree shares in the strategic allocation, a block locked for 36 months [E1][E2]. Against the 40,446,434 shares issued in the IPO, that allocation is about 2.31% of the issue: 933,399 divided by 40,446,434 is roughly 0.02308 [E1]. Against the expected enlarged capital of 404,464,340 shares, the same allocation is only about 0.2308% of the company [E1]. The 2.31% figure therefore describes DeepSeek’s share of the IPO issue, never a 2.31% company stake.

The lock-up makes the allocation more than a momentary IPO trade. The verification report gives the strategic allotment a 36-month restriction, and the legal opinion independently reproduces that term [E1][E2]. That puts DeepSeek on Unitree’s shareholder register for a defined period while preventing an immediate exit from the allocated shares [E1][E2]. Ownership, however, is only the first pipe in the arrangement.

The second pipe is procurement preference instead of technical integration. The strategic documents say the parties will choose each other as partners under equal conditions [E1]. In practice, Unitree can prefer DeepSeek when selecting model services under otherwise equal conditions, while DeepSeek can prefer Unitree when buying robots or embodied-AI solutions under the same condition [E1]. The wording creates a route into each other’s vendor queue without creating an unconditional order.

Nothing in the disclosed record sets a minimum purchase, exclusivity clause or committed procurement volume [E1][E2]. By the cutoff, the documents also identified no jointly specified model, dataset, benchmark, API, robot pilot or deployed task arising from the agreement [E1][E2]. Unitree’s public news centre showed no jointly branded launch that would supply that missing implementation layer [E3]. The plumbing stops at locked ownership plus conditional commercial preference.

That still leaves a meaningful counter-case to the boring interpretation. A 36-month locked shareholder position combined with reciprocal preference can lower the commercial friction required for one supplier to enter the other’s purchasing process, even before a public product appears [E1][E2]. If future robot deployments need external model services, or DeepSeek needs physical platforms for embodied work, each side has already documented a mechanism for favoring the other when competing offers are otherwise equal [E1]. The filing matters as supply-chain positioning even though it does not yet prove a shared stack.

The forecast assigns a 0.38 probability that by 23:59 UTC on 30 November 2026 either company publishes a jointly branded, inspectable artifact explicitly tied to the August agreement. A model or checkpoint, technical report, dataset, benchmark, API or named robot pilot settles YES; conference appearances, financing commentary, procurement preference alone and choreography do not. The call is NO because the agreement establishes access and preference without specifying a project, release obligation or timetable [E1][E2]. The absence of any jointly branded launch at the cutoff keeps the starting evidence on the commercial side of the boundary [E3].

An integrated robot stack would require another circuit: a named task, a robot producing observations, those observations entering an identified model or evaluation process, and a resulting system returning to an inspectable deployment. None of those links appears in the disclosed agreement or the public launch record by the cutoff [E1][E3]. A later purchase order could prove that the vendor preference is being exercised without proving that such a learning circuit exists. Until an artifact exposes that connection, the missing data loop remains the story.

dissent.argument: The filing sets no project, release duty or timetable; the strict four-month settlement bar excludes procurement language and demos.
